# Run the round like a sales process

Source: https://lowob.com/research/run-the-round-like-a-sales-process/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-02-19 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Treat investors as accounts. Pick them for fit, including whether the fund still has capital to deploy, research the partner, get in warm, run first meetings inside a two-to-three-week window, and track every firm through pipeline stages with pass reasons logged. In 2026, with capital concentrated in large, established funds, a fit-first list matters more than a long one.

Treat investors as accounts. Pick them for fit, research each one, get in warm, run the process in a tight window, and track every firm through stages the way a sales team tracks a pipeline. Fit now includes a question many founders skip: whether the fund still has money to invest. In 2026, managers on their fourth fund or later captured 88.2% of US venture fundraising dollars through September, and first-time funds closed at a decade-low pace.

*Not investment or legal advice. **lowob** doesn't act as a placement agent or finder and takes no percentage of anything raised.*

## 1. Build the account list

Start with fit, not fame. A fund is a fit if it has made investments at your stage, in your category, recently, and has room in its current fund. Check their last 12 months of announced deals, not their homepage.

The "room in the fund" test matters more this year. The Q3 2026 PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor found US venture funds raised $108.5 billion through September, with funds of $500 million or more taking 78.1% of it while making up 6.0% of funds closed. Only 81 first-time funds closed, on pace for a decade low. PitchBook's midyear outlook noted that emerging managers who raised in 2021 or 2022 had likely used most of their dry powder. A fund that last raised four years ago may still take meetings while reserving what it has left for its existing portfolio.

| Investor type | What it wants | What to check first |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Crypto-native fund | Protocol and token fit, ecosystem fluency | Recent deals at your stage, token allocation terms |
| Generalist with a crypto practice | A business that would work without the token cycle | Which partner leads crypto, and how often they lead |
| Ecosystem fund or foundation | Deployment on their chain | Whether the chain is the right GTM choice, not just the right cheque |
| AI infrastructure fund | Compute, tooling, model-layer economics | Whether it has backed applications at all |
| AI application fund | Workflow ownership, retention, margin | Recent application deals in your buyer's category |

For web3: separate crypto-native funds, generalist funds with a crypto practice, and ecosystem funds or foundations attached to a chain. Each wants a different story. Ecosystem money often wants deployment on their chain; that's a GTM decision, not just a funding one.

For AI: separate funds that back infrastructure from those that back applications. An application company pitching an infrastructure fund will hear "interesting, but not for us" for three weeks.

Tier the list. Tier 1 is 10 to 15 firms you'd be thrilled to have lead. Tier 2 is the next 20 to 30. Don't pitch Tier 1 first; practise on early Tier 2 meetings for a week.

## 2. Research the partner, not the firm

Find the person at the firm who invests in your area. Read what they've written and what they've backed. Your first email should name one specific reason you're relevant to *them*.

Concentration applies inside firms too. PitchBook's midyear outlook counted 74 seed, Series A and Series B deals by one large multi-stage firm in 2026 by mid-June. At that pace a partner sees many decks a week. The specific reason in your first line is what separates yours from the rest.

## 3. Get in warm

The best introduction is from a founder in their portfolio who knows your product. Next best: an operator or angel they trust. A cold email with sharp evidence ([Raise against evidence, not narrative](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/)) still works better than a lukewarm intro from someone who barely knows you.

Make intros easy. Send the introducer a forwardable three-line email: who you are, what you've proven, why this investor. The same logic drives [signal-based outbound](https://lowob.com/research/signal-based-outbound/) in sales: a real reason to talk beats volume.

## 4. Compress the window

Run first meetings within two to three weeks. Overlapping interest is what creates urgency; a raise that drips out over four months signals that nobody wants it.

The cost of a slow round has grown. Carta's first-quarter 2026 data puts the median gap between seed and Series A at two years, and between Series A and Series B at 2.1 years. A round that takes six months to close eats a quarter of the runway it was raised to fund.

> If three firms pass for the same reason, that's not investor taste. It's a gap in your evidence or story.

## 5. Track it like a pipeline

| Stage | Meaning | Next action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Researched | Fit confirmed, partner identified | Find the warm route |
| Intro requested | Forwardable email sent to introducer | Follow up in 5 days |
| First meeting | Taken | Send follow-up and homework within 48 hours |
| Partner / deep dive | Second meeting or diligence | Data room access, customer references |
| Term sheet | Offer in hand | Legal review |
| Passed | Declined | Log the reason in their words |

Write the stage definitions down before the first meeting, the way a sales team writes [pipeline stage definitions](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/), so "first meeting" means the same thing every time you count it.

The "passed" reasons are gold. If three firms pass for the same reason, that's not investor taste; it's a gap in your evidence or story. Treat each one as a [closed-lost reason](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-closed-lost-reason/): recorded at the time, in the investor's words, with a category you can count later. When the round goes quiet, those reasons are the first thing to read, as [The round has stalled](https://lowob.com/research/the-round-has-stalled/) sets out.

## 6. Have the data room ready before the first meeting

Deck, a one-page memo, the model, the cap table (and token allocation for web3), the evidence log, audits or security reviews, and two or three customers willing to take a reference call. Diligence that waits on you kills momentum.

| Data room item | Why it is there before meeting one |
| --- | --- |
| Deck and one-page memo | Partners forward the memo internally, not the deck |
| Model | The first homework request is usually the model |
| Cap table and token allocation | Ownership questions stop rounds late if they arrive late |
| Evidence log | Shows the dated record behind every traction claim |
| Audits or security reviews | Removes a diligence step that otherwise takes weeks |
| Two or three reference customers | Lets an investor hear the evidence from someone else |

## lowob takeaways

- **Fit includes capital.** Check recent deals at your stage and whether the current fund has room to invest.
- **Research the partner.** One specific reason in the first line beats a generic email to a famous firm.
- **Compress the window.** First meetings inside two to three weeks create the overlap that produces decisions.
- **Log every pass in the investor's words.** Matching reasons are the clearest signal the round will give you.

## Next move

Take your current investor list and add two columns: the date of each fund's last deal at your stage, and the year its current fund closed. Cut every fund that fails either test before you send a single email.
